description:
We are Brand House, a multidisciplinary team combining communication, product strategy, UX/UI design, software development, and data visualization.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we aim to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data to analyze wildfire patterns in the Peruvian Amazon.

We welcome collaborators skilled in GIS, Python, satellite data, remote sensing, Earth science, and environmental research.
summary:
FIRE SCOPE is a global platform designed to harmonize NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite hot spot data, helping users explore and understand fire activity across the world.

It addresses the challenge of comparing observations from two sensors with different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities by applying quality filtering, aggregating detections into approximately 1 km daily grid cells, and calibrating VIIRS data against MODIS during their overlapping period.

The platform transforms these observations into a continuous historical time series, enabling users to explore fire activity through interactive maps, monthly calendars, historical anomalies, seasonal patterns, cumulative trends, and year-to-year comparisons. Its geographic framework is designed to support analysis at multiple levels, from countries and their first-level administrative divisions, such as departments, states, and regions, to provinces, districts, and other local areas, where reliable geographic boundary data are available.

FIRE SCOPE also features Aura, a virtual assistant that helps users interpret the information displayed by the platform. By making satellite data easier to explore and understand, FIRE SCOPE supports more informed monitoring and awareness of fire activity worldwide.
details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

FIRE SCOPE is a global geospatial analysis platform that harmonizes satellite-based active fire and thermal anomaly data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS sensors, enabling users to explore, analyze, and understand fire activity over time.

The project addresses an important challenge: although both sensors detect thermal anomalies, they have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities. MODIS provides observations at approximately 1 km resolution dating back to 2000, while VIIRS offers a resolution of 375 meters starting in 2012. For this reason, their detection counts cannot be directly compared.

To address this problem, FIRE SCOPE implements a harmonization process that includes:

• Data ingestion: retrieves historical records through NASA FIRMS
Archive Download and recent observations through the FIRMS Area API.
• Quality filtering: normalizes the confidence levels of both sensors and
removes low-confidence detections.
• Spatial normalization: groups detections into approximately 1 km cells
per day, reducing differences caused by the sensors' distinct spatial
resolutions.
• Local calibration: calculates equivalence factors between MODIS and
VIIRS during their overlapping operational period, using the records
available for each analyzed area.
• Continuous historical time series: uses MODIS for the period before
2012 and calibrated VIIRS data for the period thereafter, maintaining
continuity in historical analysis.

The processed information is presented through an interactive platform that integrates a geospatial viewer, monthly calendars, historical anomaly analysis, seasonal patterns, year-to-year comparisons, and cumulative trends. Users can also select areas of interest by drawing on the map, entering coordinates, or selecting administrative jurisdictions; explore recent detections; export data in CSV and GeoJSON formats; and generate PDF situation reports.

FIRE SCOPE also features Aura, a virtual analyst that allows users to interact with the platform through natural language queries and receive responses in both text and voice. Aura helps users interpret the platform's data and results by using figures retrieved directly from the system's analytical tools, avoiding the generation of unverified statistics.

The analytical engine has global reach and allows users to query any area of the planet through geographic selection. As its first national geographic implementation, FIRE SCOPE provides a comprehensive experience for Peru, including its 25 departments and administrative boundaries. This architecture allows the analysis to be extended to the administrative divisions of other countries by integrating their corresponding geographic data.

What benefits does the project offer?

FIRE SCOPE transforms large volumes of satellite observations into organized, accessible, and understandable information.

Its main benefits include:

• Enables users to explore a harmonized historical time series dating back
to the early 2000s.
• Facilitates temporal and geographic comparisons of detections, reducing
biases associated with differences between sensors.
• Helps identify historical anomalies, seasonal patterns, and variations in
hot spot activity.
• Allows users to analyze specific geographic areas and explore territorial
information.
• Facilitates data downloads and report generation for research and
further analysis.
• Incorporates a virtual assistant that helps interpret results through
natural language queries and text and voice responses.
• Integrates satellite data, geospatial processing, and historical analysis
into a single platform.

What is the expected impact of the project?

FIRE SCOPE aims to contribute to more informed monitoring of hot spot activity and a better understanding of its historical evolution.

Its potential reach is global, as it allows users to analyze areas anywhere on the planet using NASA satellite data. Its first national geographic implementation focuses on Peru, with an architecture designed to progressively expand administrative coverage to other countries.

The platform can be used by researchers, universities, and academic centers, particularly in the fields of environmental engineering, forestry engineering, geography, geomatics, biology, ecology, agronomy, forest sciences, and disaster risk management. It can also serve public institutions, environmental organizations, territorial management teams, journalists, and citizens interested in understanding fire activity.

Its purpose is to make historical and recent information more accessible to support research, territorial monitoring, and decision-making.

FIRE SCOPE recognizes that a satellite detection represents a thermal anomaly and does not, by itself, confirm the presence of a fire. Therefore, results require interpretation and, when appropriate, field verification.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used?

Backend and data processing:
• Python 3.12
• FastAPI
• Uvicorn
• pandas
• NumPy
• SQLite with WAL mode
• httpx for external service requests.

Geospatial processing:
• Shapely 2
• GeoJSON
• Leaflet 1.9.4
• Leaflet.draw.

Frontend and interface design:
• Vanilla JavaScript
• HTML and CSS
• Custom SVG graphics
• Plus Jakarta Sans
• CSS variables for visual themes and responsive design.

Artificial intelligence:
• Anthropic Claude SDK and API (Haiku/Opus), integrated into Aura, the
virtual analyst.
• AI tools used to support programming, code generation and debugging,
and prototype testing.
• Image and video generation tools used to create Aura's visual assets.

Infrastructure and deployment:
• Docker
• Docker Compose
• nginx
• Let's Encrypt for HTTPS implementation.
• ReportLab for PDF report generation.

Satellite data sources:
• NASA FIRMS.
• MODIS C6.1 (MCD14ML).
• VIIRS 375 m (VNP14IMGTML and VJ114IMGTML).
• NASA GIBS and Worldview.

The project also uses administrative geographic boundaries from Peru's National Institute of Statistics and Informatics (INEI), basemaps from Esri and OpenStreetMap, and open-source software libraries.

In what ways is the project creative and innovative?

FIRE SCOPE's main innovation lies in addressing the historical continuity problem between two generations of satellite sensors with different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities.

Instead of directly comparing MODIS and VIIRS detection counts, the system applies spatial normalization and local calibration to build a harmonized historical time series. This helps reduce differences between sensors and maintain analytical continuity as MODIS approaches the end of its operational life.

Another innovative aspect is the integration of multiple tools into a single experience: satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, historical exploration, anomaly identification, temporal comparisons, report generation, and data exports.

In addition, FIRE SCOPE features Aura, a virtual analyst that allows users to interact with data through natural language and receive text and voice responses. Its operation is based on querying information processed by the system and presenting verified figures, preventing artificial intelligence from inventing data.

By combining satellite science, data harmonization, geospatial analysis, and artificial intelligence, FIRE SCOPE makes complex environmental information easier to explore and understand.

What factors did the team consider?

The team primarily considered the quality, availability, and origin of satellite data; the technical differences between MODIS and VIIRS; the continuity of historical records; and the accuracy of geographic analysis.

The team also prioritized ease of use, map accessibility, area-of-interest selection, data downloads, and report generation.

Methodological transparency was incorporated through features such as identifying incomplete periods, displaying the calibration factor, providing warnings about the limitations of satellite detections, and recognizing that weather conditions, particularly cloud cover, can obscure hot spots.

Finally, the team developed a scalable architecture that allows analysis of areas anywhere in the world and the progressive expansion of the platform's administrative geographic coverage.
